why.correct: Average rate = −Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = −(0.134 M − 0.200 M)/(200 s − 0 s) = 0.066 M / 200 s = 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. The difference 0.066 M has two significant figures, so the rate does too.
Each 2 mol of N₂O₅ that react make 4 mol of NO₂, so NO₂ appears 4/2 = 2 times as fast as N₂O₅ disappears: 2 × 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ M/s = 6.6 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.

The data show the concentration falling, and the drop per 100 s shrinking (0.036 M, then 0.030 M, 0.024 M, 0.020 M). With fewer N₂O₅ molecules per liter, fewer react each second, so the rate falls as the reactant is used up.
options: Right: the rate depends on how much reactant is present, and the concentration of N₂O₅ keeps falling.
Products do not "use up heat", and the stem says the temperature is constant. This invents a cause the data do not show.
The stem says the temperature is constant, so a temperature change cannot explain the data.
A sealed flask keeps the gas in; it does not stop molecules from reacting. The rate falls because the reactant concentration falls.

why.correct: One O₂ forms for every 2 N₂O₅ used, so O₂ appears half as fast: 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ M/s ÷ 2 = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
options: Right: the 1 : 2 ratio of the coefficients halves the rate.
This treats every species as changing at the same rate, ignoring the coefficients.
This multiplies by 2, as if O₂ had the larger coefficient. It has the smaller one (1 vs 2).
This is the rate for NO₂ (4 per 2 N₂O₅), not for O₂.

why.correct: The powder curve is much steeper near t = 0 (about 57 mL in the first 15 s against about 25 mL for the chips). Powder exposes far more surface, so more CaCO₃ particles meet acid particles each second.
options: Right: steeper initial slope, explained by surface area.
Only particles at the surface of a solid can meet the acid. Big chips hide most of their particles inside.
Grinding is a physical change; powdered marble is still CaCO₃.
Equal masses give equal amounts of product in the end, not equal rates. The slopes at the start are clearly different.

why.correct: The acid is in excess, so CaCO₃ is the limiting reactant. 0.33 g of CaCO₃ (about 0.0033 mol) makes the same amount of CO₂ however fast it reacts. Rate is how fast product forms; the amount is set by stoichiometry.
options: Right: rate changes how quickly you get there, not how much you get.
The stem says the acid is in excess, so it does not run out; the marble does.
A faster reaction does not make more product. Nothing in the data shows gas escaping.
This is the mix-up the question targets: rate is amount per unit time; the final amount is set by the limiting reactant.

why.correct: At 60 s the chips curve reads 62 mL; at 0 s it reads 0 mL. Average rate = (62 mL − 0 mL)/(60 s − 0 s) = 1.0 mL/s. A reading a millilitre or two either way still rounds to about 1.0 mL/s.
More concentrated acid puts more acid particles next to the marble surface, so more react each second. The marble is still the limiting reactant, so the final volume is unchanged.
options: Right: higher concentration raises the rate; the amount of marble, which sets the yield, stays the same.
More marble would raise the final volume, since marble is the limiting reactant.
One lump has less surface than several chips, so it would react more slowly.
Water dilutes the acid, which lowers the rate.

why.correct: Δ[NH₃]/Δt = (2 mol NH₃ / 3 mol H₂) × 0.090 M/s = 0.060 M/s.
M/s is (mol/L) per second: how much a concentration changes each second.
options: Right: rate is concentration change per unit time.
That is an amount of product, set by stoichiometry, not a rate.
Energy per second would be in J/s, not M/s.
A time would be in seconds alone, not M/s.

why.correct: Divide each rate by its coefficient, and put a minus sign on reactants so the rate is positive: −½ Δ[N₂O]/Δt = ½ Δ[N₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt.
options: Right: each change divided by its coefficient, with a minus sign for the reactant.
Multiplying by the coefficients makes the fastest-changing species look even faster; you divide instead.
This ignores the coefficients and the sign: N₂O falls while the others rise, and O₂ changes half as fast.
N₂ is a product, so its concentration rises; a minus sign would make its rate negative.

why.correct: Surface area changes how fast the zinc reacts, not how much reacts: the rate goes up and the time goes down, while the amounts stay the same.

variables.name: Initial rate of hydrogen production
variables.why: Powder has much more surface touching the acid, so more zinc atoms react each second.

variables.name: Total volume of hydrogen made
variables.why: The same mass of zinc (the limiting reactant) reacts, so the same amount of hydrogen forms.

variables.name: Time for all the zinc to dissolve
variables.why: A faster rate uses up the same amount of zinc sooner.

variables.name: Mass of zinc that reacts
variables.why: All 1.0 g reacts in both cases because the acid is in excess.

why.correct: Warmer particles move faster and collide harder and more often; more concentrated acid puts more acid particles at the metal surface. A wider beaker changes neither; water dilutes the acid.
options: Right: a higher temperature raises the rate.
Right: a higher concentration raises the rate.
The concentration and the metal surface are the same, so the rate is unchanged.
Diluting lowers the concentration of acid, which slows the reaction.

why.correct: The instantaneous rate is the slope of the curve at one moment, which is the slope of the tangent line there. The reactant falls, so the slope is negative and the rate is its negative.
options: Right: the slope of the tangent at that time, made positive for a reactant.
A rate is a change divided by a time, not a concentration divided by a time.
That gives the average rate over the whole run, not the rate at 50 s.
A concentration is not a rate; the rate is how fast the concentration changes.

why.correct: By the Beer-Lambert law, absorbance is proportional to concentration at a fixed wavelength and path length. A larger drop in absorbance in the same 10 s means a larger drop in concentration, so the rate is greater at the start.
options: Right: A = εbc lets absorbance stand in for concentration.
The smaller drop near 60 s means a smaller change per second, which is a slower rate.
Absorbance is proportional to concentration (A = εbc), so its changes track the rate.
Different drops in equal times mean different rates.

why.correct: Rate = amount formed ÷ time. X: 25 mL ÷ 50 s = 0.50 mL/s. Y: 50 mL ÷ 50 s = 1.0 mL/s. The higher concentration doubled the rate.
options: Right: equal times, double the gas, double the rate.
Measuring for different times would make the comparison harder, not fix it.
Gas volumes measured the same way can be compared directly; that is how the rate is found.
The rates are 0.50 mL/s and 1.0 mL/s, which are not equal.

why.correct: Change in moles = 0.0800 − 0.0560 = 0.0240 mol; change in concentration = 0.0240 mol / 0.250 L = 0.0960 M. Rate = 0.0960 M / 40.0 s = 2.40 × 10⁻³ M/s. The subtraction leaves 0.0240 (three significant figures), so the answer has three.
Compare trials 1 and 2, where only [NO] changes: [NO] doubles and the rate goes from 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ to 7.20 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, a factor of 4. Since 2ᵐ = 4, m = 2.
options: Zero order would leave the rate unchanged when [NO] changes.
First order would double the rate when [NO] doubles; here it quadruples.
Right: doubling [NO] multiplies the rate by 4 = 2².
Third order would multiply the rate by 2³ = 8.

why.correct: Compare trials 1 and 3, where only [Cl₂] changes: it doubles and the rate doubles (1.80 → 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ M/s). 2ⁿ = 2 gives n = 1.
options: Zero order would leave the rate unchanged; it doubled.
Half order would multiply the rate by about 1.4, not 2.
Right: the rate changes by the same factor as [Cl₂].
Second order would quadruple the rate when [Cl₂] doubles.

why.correct: rate = k[NO]²[Cl₂], so k = rate / ([NO]²[Cl₂]) = (1.80 × 10⁻⁴ M/s) / ((0.0100 M)²(0.0100 M)) = (1.80 × 10⁻⁴ M/s) / (1.00 × 10⁻⁶ M³) = 1.80 × 10² M⁻² s⁻¹. The units are M/s ÷ M³ = M⁻² s⁻¹.

rate = k[NO]²[Cl₂] = (180 M⁻² s⁻¹)(0.0300 M)²(0.0050 M) = (180)(9.00 × 10⁻⁴)(0.0050) M/s = 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. By ratios: [NO] ×3 gives ×9, [Cl₂] ×½ gives ×½, and 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ × 4.5 = 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. Two significant figures, from 0.0050 M.

The balanced equation shows how much reacts in total, not how the rate depends on each concentration. Here the measured orders (2 and 1) happen to equal the coefficients; for many reactions they do not, so the orders must come from experiment.
options: Right: orders are measured; a match with coefficients is a coincidence for an overall equation.
This is the misconception: the overall equation does not tell you the orders.
Product coefficients do not set the orders either; orders are found by experiment.
Being gases makes no difference; orders still come from data.

why.correct: Trials 1 and 2: [X] doubles, rate doubles, so first order in X. Trials 1 and 3: [Y] triples, rate is unchanged, so zero order in Y ([Y]⁰ = 1). rate = k[X].
options: Right: first order in X, zero order in Y.
Tripling [Y] would triple the rate; the data show no change.
The rate does not change with [Y] but does change with [X].
Doubling [X] would quadruple the rate; it only doubles.

why.correct: Zero order in Y means changing [Y] does not change the rate. Y can still be consumed; it simply is not involved in whatever controls the speed (topic 5.8 explains how a mechanism can leave a reactant out of the rate law).
options: Right: zero order means the rate does not depend on [Y], not that Y is not used.
Y is listed as a reactant and is consumed; zero order only means its concentration does not set the rate.
Y is on the reactant side of the equation.
The stem says Y is dissolved; its concentration was varied from 0.15 M to 0.45 M.

why.correct: k = rate / [X] = (2.4 × 10⁻⁵ M/s) / (0.15 M) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. For a first-order rate law the units are M/s ÷ M = s⁻¹.
rate = k[X] = (1.6 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹)(0.45 M) = 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ M/s. [Y] is zero order, so its value does not matter.
The overall order is 1 + 2 = 3. k = rate/([A][B]²) has units (M/s)/M³ = M⁻² s⁻¹.
options: These are the units of a rate, which is also the units of k for zero order.
These are the units for a first-order rate law.
These are the units for a second-order rate law.
Right: third order overall gives M⁻² s⁻¹.

why.correct: Doubling [B] alone doubles the rate (first order). The rest of the factor of 8 comes from A: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 = 2², so the order in A is 2.
options: Zero order in A would make the total change only 2.
First order in both would give 2 × 2 = 4, not 8.
Right: 2ᵐ × 2¹ = 8 gives m = 2.
This puts the whole factor of 8 on A and forgets the doubling from B.

why.correct: The rate goes up by 2² = 4. The rate constant and the order stay the same: k changes only with temperature (or a new pathway).

variables.name: Initial rate
variables.why: The rate depends on [NO₂]², so doubling [NO₂] multiplies the rate by 4.

variables.name: Rate constant k
variables.why: k depends on temperature and the reaction, not on concentration.

variables.name: Overall order of the reaction
variables.why: The order is a property of the rate law (2 here); it does not change with concentration.

why.correct: k depends on temperature. Changing a concentration changes the rate, not k; orders need not match overall coefficients; and the units of k depend on the overall order.
options: Right: k is a constant at one temperature only.
Concentration changes the rate; k stays the same at a given temperature.
Orders often differ from the overall coefficients; they must be measured.
The units of k depend on the overall order: s⁻¹ for first order, M⁻¹ s⁻¹ for second order.

why.correct: Zero order: rate = k[A]⁰ = k. The rate does not depend on [A], so it stays constant until the reactant runs out. k then has the units of a rate, M/s.
options: Right: a zero-order rate is independent of concentration.
That describes a first-order reactant.
Zero order does not mean "does not react"; it means the rate does not depend on [A].
s⁻¹ is the unit of a first-order k; a zero-order k is in M/s.

why.correct: To isolate one order, change only that concentration and hold everything else constant. The ratio of initial rates then depends only on [B].
options: Right: one variable at a time.
The coefficient does not give the order; it must be measured.
Changing both at once mixes their effects (unless one order is already known).
Changing temperature changes k, which says nothing about the order in B.

why.correct: ln[C₃H₆] goes −3.00, −3.30, −3.60, −3.90, −4.19: it falls by about 0.30 each 500 s, so a plot of ln[C₃H₆] against time is a straight line, which means first order. 1/[C₃H₆] rises by more each interval (20.0, 27.0, 36.5, 49.3, 66.2), so that plot curves.
options: Right: equal steps in ln[A] in equal times means ln[A] vs t is linear, which is first order.
1/[A] rises, but by growing amounts (not equal steps), so 1/[A] vs t is not linear; it is not second order.
[A] falls by shrinking amounts (0.0130, 0.0096, ...), so [A] vs t is curved; it is not zero order.
This is the claim readers do not accept: it does not say which graph is linear. Name the plot, ln[A] against time.

why.correct: For first order, ln[A] vs t has slope −k. k = −(ln[A]₂₀₀₀ − ln[A]₀)/(2000 s − 0 s) = −(−4.19 − (−3.00))/2000 s = 1.19/2000 s = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹.
t½ = 0.693 / k = 0.693 / (6.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) = 1155 s, which is 1.2 × 10³ s to two significant figures. Check with the table: [C₃H₆] falls from 0.0500 M to 0.0250 M somewhere between 1000 s and 1500 s.
A straight line for 1/[A] against time is the signature of second order (1/[A]t = kt + 1/[A]₀). The justification names the plot that is linear.
options: Right: names the linear plot and draws the right conclusion.
Zero order would make [NO₂] against time linear, not 1/[NO₂].
First order would make ln[NO₂] against time linear.
1/[NO₂] rises because [NO₂] falls; NO₂ is the reactant.

why.correct: For second order, slope of 1/[A] vs t = k. Slope = (75 M⁻¹ − 25 M⁻¹)/(100 s − 0 s) = 0.50 M⁻¹ s⁻¹.

From 0.0400 to 0.0200 M: (50 − 25)/0.50 = 50 s. From 0.0200 to 0.0100 M: (100 − 50)/0.50 = 100 s. For second order the halving time doubles each time, because the rate falls with the square of the concentration.
options: Right: 50 s, then 100 s.
A constant half-life belongs to first-order reactions only.
Less reactant means a slower rate, so halving takes longer, not shorter.
k is constant, but for second order the half-life also depends on [A].

why.correct: [NH₃] against time is linear, so the rate (the slope) is the same at every concentration: zero order. For first or second order, [A] against time curves.
options: Right: the linear plot named is [A] vs t, which is zero order.
A first-order reaction gives a curve for [A] vs t; ln[A] vs t would be the straight one.
A second-order reaction gives a curve for [A] vs t; 1/[A] vs t would be the straight one.
The rate is constant until the NH₃ runs out; that is why the line is straight.

why.correct: Slope = (0.0000 M − 0.0200 M)/(80 s − 0 s) = −2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. For zero order, slope = −k, so k = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
Δ[H₂]/Δt = (3/2)(2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s) = 3.75 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, which is 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ M/s to two significant figures.
When every spot on the surface is occupied, adding more NH₃ to the gas cannot speed things up: the number of reacting molecules per second is set by the surface, so the rate does not depend on [NH₃].
options: Right: a saturated surface makes the rate independent of the gas concentration.
If NH₃ molecules reacted with each other in the gas, the rate would depend on [NH₃].
The wire is not a reactant in 2 NH₃ → N₂ + 3 H₂.
If everything reacted at once, the concentration would drop to zero at once, not along a line.

why.correct: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% is three half-lives: 3 × 8.02 days = 24.1 days. Radioactive decay is first order, so every half-life is the same length.
Doubling [A]₀ doubles the rate, but k, the half-life and the slope of the ln[A] plot all stay the same.

variables.name: Initial rate
variables.why: rate = k[A], so doubling [A] doubles the initial rate.

variables.name: Half-life
variables.why: For first order t½ = 0.693/k, which does not depend on concentration.

variables.name: Rate constant k
variables.why: k depends on temperature, which is unchanged.

variables.name: Slope of ln[A] against time
variables.why: The slope is −k, and k is unchanged; the line just starts higher.

why.correct: First order: ln[A] vs t, slope −k. Second order: 1/[A] vs t, slope +k. Zero order: [A] vs t, slope −k.
options: Right: the first-order plot falls with slope −k.
1/[A] rises over time, so its slope is +k, not −k.
For first order, [A] vs t curves; only ln[A] vs t is straight.
ln[A] vs t is the first-order plot, and it falls.

why.correct: k = 0.693 / t½ = 0.693 / 45 s = 0.0154 s⁻¹, which is 0.015 s⁻¹ to two significant figures.
For an elementary step the rate law comes straight from the step: one A and one B collide, so rate = k[A][B].
options: Right: first order in each of the two colliding reactants.
AB is the product; a rate law uses the reactants.
That would describe two A molecules colliding.
Rate laws multiply concentrations; they are not sums.

why.correct: Box 2 has twice as many A molecules and the same number of B. With rate = k[A][B], doubling [A] doubles the rate: there are twice as many possible A–B pairs to collide.
options: Box 2 has more molecules, not fewer.
More A molecules means more A–B collisions per second.
Right: [A] doubles, [B] stays the same.
Four times would need both [A] and [B] doubled, as in Box 3.

why.correct: Both [A] and [B] double: rate × 2 × 2 = 4. Box 1 has 2 × 2 = 4 possible A–B pairs; Box 3 has 4 × 4 = 16.
options: More molecules of both kinds means more collisions.
That counts only the doubling of one reactant.
Right: 2 × 2 = 4.
That would be a third-order step.

why.correct: Molecularity counts the reactant particles that come together in the step: one A and one B, two particles.
options: Every elementary step involves at least one particle.
Unimolecular is one particle changing on its own.
Right: two particles collide.
Termolecular needs three particles colliding at once.

why.correct: Two NO₂ molecules collide in this step, so the rate is proportional to [NO₂] × [NO₂] = [NO₂]².
options: Right: the coefficient 2 becomes the exponent for an elementary step.
That would be a single NO₂ falling apart.
Those are the products; a forward rate law uses reactants.
The coefficient goes in the exponent, not in front of k.

why.correct: Step 4 needs two NO molecules and one O₂ to meet at once: three particles.
options: Step 1 is one O₃ breaking apart: unimolecular.
Step 2 is NO meeting O₃: bimolecular.
Step 3 is two NO₂ meeting: bimolecular.
Right: 2 NO + O₂ is three particles.

why.correct: A collision of two particles is common; having a third arrive at exactly the same moment is far less likely, so steps with three particles are rare.
options: Right: a three-body collision is improbable.
Energy is not the reason; the meeting itself is unlikely.
Step 4 is a gas-phase step; molecularity is not about the state.
Orientation is a separate issue; the main problem is getting three together at once.

why.correct: Step 1 is unimolecular: rate = k[O₃]. Tripling [O₃] triples the rate.
options: The rate of a unimolecular step depends on how many molecules are there.
Right: first order in O₃.
9 would need the step to be second order in O₃.
27 would need third order.

why.correct: If the overall equation were one elementary step, the rate law would be k[H₂]²[NO]². The measured order in H₂ is 1, so the reaction happens in more than one step (a mechanism, topic 5.7).
options: Right: an elementary rate law follows its coefficients, and this one does not.
Four particles meeting at once is essentially impossible; the data also rule it out.
Measured orders are the facts; it is the "single step" idea that fails.
This is the misconception: only elementary steps follow their coefficients.

why.correct: An elementary reaction is one event, so its rate law can be written from its coefficients. An overall equation is often several steps, and steps of four or more particles do not happen.
options: Right: one event at the particle level.
Right: for a single event, the coefficients give the orders.
Only elementary steps can be read this way; overall rate laws must be measured.
Almost all elementary steps are uni- or bimolecular; three is rare and four essentially unknown.

why.correct: Second order in X with nothing else means two X particles collide: 2 X → products.
options: Right: two X collide.
One X breaking apart is first order in X.
That step would be first order in X and first order in Y.
One X₂ breaking apart would be first order in X₂.

why.correct: Fewer NO₂ molecules means fewer NO₂–NO₂ collisions: the rate drops to a quarter. k and the molecularity are unchanged.

variables.name: Rate of the step
variables.why: rate = k[NO₂]², so halving [NO₂] cuts the rate to (½)² = ¼.

variables.name: Rate constant k
variables.why: k depends on temperature, not on concentration.

variables.name: Molecularity of the step
variables.why: The step still involves two NO₂ molecules colliding; molecularity is a property of the step.

why.correct: Halving the volume doubles every concentration. The step is bimolecular, rate = k[H][Cl₂], so the rate changes by 2 × 2 = 4: each H atom meets Cl₂ molecules twice as often, and there are twice as many H atoms per liter.
options: The same molecules in less space collide more often.
That counts only one of the two concentrations.
Right: both concentrations double.
Eight would need a termolecular step.

why.correct: One NO and one Cl₂ collide, so each is first order: rate = k[NO][Cl₂].
options: Right: one of each reactant.
With 2 NO the rate law would be k[NO]²[Cl₂].
Its reactants are NOCl and Cl, so its rate law is k[NOCl][Cl].
Its rate law would be k[NOCl]².

why.correct: At a higher temperature the average kinetic energy is larger, so the distribution shifts right and spreads out; with the same number of molecules, its peak is lower. That describes T₂.
options: Right: shifted and spread toward higher energy.
A taller, narrower peak at low energy means a lower temperature.
Many molecules at low energy means a lower average kinetic energy, so a lower temperature.
It is the same sample, so both curves represent the same number of molecules (equal areas).

why.correct: The area under each curve to the right of 20 kJ/mol is the fraction of molecules with enough energy to react. It is much larger for T₂, so a larger fraction of collisions succeeds.
options: Right: more of the curve lies beyond the activation energy.
Heating does not change the activation energy; it changes how many molecules can reach it.
Even at T₂, many molecules have less than 20 kJ/mol; the curve starts near zero.
Temperature does not change the size of molecules.

why.correct: A modest rise in temperature raises the collision frequency by a few percent, but it can multiply the fraction of molecules with energy above Ea several times over (compare the tails of the two curves beyond 20 kJ/mol). The energy effect dominates.
options: Right: the high-energy tail grows sharply.
Collision frequency does rise, but only a little compared with the growth of the high-energy tail.
The energy effect is much larger for reactions with a significant activation energy.
The activation energy is a property of the pathway; heating does not change it.

why.correct: The area under a distribution curve between two energies is the fraction of molecules with energies in that range. Molecules beyond 20 kJ/mol can react if they also collide with the right orientation.
options: Right: the tail beyond the activation energy.
The peak height is the fraction at the most common energy, not a count above Ea.
The peak energy is the most probable energy, which is well below Ea here.
Those are the molecules without enough energy to react.

why.correct: To form Cl₂, the incoming Cl must meet the Cl of NOCl. A collision at the O end, however energetic, puts the atoms in the wrong places, so the molecules bounce apart.
options: Right: enough energy and the right orientation.
The O end is far from the Cl atom that must be taken, so this orientation cannot make Cl₂.
Energy is necessary but not enough; orientation matters too.
The step is bimolecular; two particles are enough.

why.correct: A collision is effective only if it has at least the activation energy and the right orientation. Most collisions miss one or both.
options: Right: not enough energy.
Right: wrong orientation.
Gas molecules collide billions of times per second; the rate limit is not the number of collisions.
Mass is conserved in collisions.

why.correct: Heating raises both the collision frequency and the share of energetic collisions; the activation energy and the orientation requirement stay the same.

variables.name: Number of collisions per second
variables.why: Faster molecules meet more often (a small increase).

variables.name: Fraction of collisions with energy at or above Ea
variables.why: The energy distribution shifts toward higher energy, so more of it lies beyond Ea.

variables.name: Activation energy
variables.why: Ea is a property of the reaction pathway, not of the temperature.

variables.name: Fraction of collisions with a suitable orientation
variables.why: Orientation depends on the shapes of the molecules, not on how fast they move.

why.correct: The collision model needs both: enough energy to break and rearrange bonds, and the right atoms facing each other.
options: Right: both conditions.
Energy alone is not enough; the wrong orientation bounces apart.
Orientation alone is not enough; a gentle bump does not break bonds.
Mass is not a requirement for an effective collision.

why.correct: Lower temperature shifts the energy distribution to lower energies, so a much smaller fraction of collisions reaches Ea, and the spoiling reactions slow down.
options: Right: fewer energetic collisions.
The activation energy is set by the reaction pathway; temperature does not change it.
Molecules still move at refrigerator temperatures; they just move more slowly.
Cold air is slightly denser, which would speed reactions with oxygen, not slow them.

why.correct: At one temperature the energy distribution is the same, so a larger fraction of molecules is above 40 kJ/mol than above 90 kJ/mol. More effective collisions means a faster reaction and a larger k.
options: Right: lower barrier, more successful collisions.
Ea is a barrier to overcome, not energy given to the molecules.
Same temperature does not mean same rate; the barriers differ.
Ea does not change how often molecules collide.

why.correct: Concentration changes how often particles meet, not how hard they hit. More collisions per second means more effective collisions per second, at the same fraction.
options: Right: collision frequency rises.
Energy per collision depends on temperature, not concentration.
Ea does not depend on concentration.
The fraction with a good orientation is unchanged; only the number of collisions rises.

why.correct: Effective collisions = (total collisions) × (fraction with enough energy) × (fraction correctly oriented) = (3.0 × 10³¹ s⁻¹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁵)(0.15) = 9.0 × 10²⁵ per second.
Activation energy belongs to the reaction pathway. Heating shifts the distribution of molecular energies so that a larger fraction of collisions clears the same barrier.
options: Right: same barrier, more molecules over it.
The barrier is not lowered by heat; that is the misconception.
Ea does not change with temperature in either direction.
Collision frequency rises only slightly; the big effect is the energy distribution.

why.correct: Only particles at the surface of a solid can collide with the dissolved reactant. Grinding exposes far more of them, so the number of collisions per second rises; the energy of each collision and Ea are unchanged.
options: Right: more surface, more collisions.
Collision energy depends on temperature, not on particle size.
Ea is a property of the reaction pathway; grinding does not change it.
Grinding changes how many particles are exposed, not how each collision is aimed.

why.correct: Ea (forward) = E(transition state) − E(reactants) = 150 kJ/mol − 40 kJ/mol = 110 kJ/mol.

Run in reverse, the reaction starts at the products and climbs to the same transition state: Ea (reverse) = 150 − 10 = 140 kJ/mol. Check: Ea(reverse) − Ea(forward) = 140 − 110 = 30, the size of the energy released.
The peak is the transition state, the highest-energy arrangement along the path. It lasts for about one molecular vibration and cannot be isolated.
